readings.c2s1:
¶
'''untowardness''' (un-tō′ärd-nes), ''n.'' The state or character of being untoward; awkwardness; frowardness; perverseness. ''Bp. Wilson.''

'''untowen†''', '''untown†''', ''a.'' [ME., also ''untohen'', ''untohe'', < AS. ''ungetogen'' (= MLG. ''untogen'', MHG. ''ungezogen''), uninstructed, untaught, < ''un-'', not, + ''togen'', pp. of ''teón'', draw, educate, instruct: see ''un-'' and ''tee''<sup>1</sup>, and cf. ''wanton'', earlier ''wantowen''.] Untaught; untrained; rude.

'''untowered''' (un-tou′ėrd), ''a.'' Not having towers; not defended by towers. ''Wordsworth.''

'''untrace''' (un-trās′), ''v. t.'' To loose from the traces or drawing-straps: as, to ''untrace'' a horse.
{{smaller block|<poem>And now the fiery horses of the Sun
Were from their golden-flaming car ''untrac’d.''</poem>
{{right|''Middleton'', Father Hubbard’s Tales.}}}}

'''untraceable''' (un-trā′sạ-bl), ''a.'' Incapable of being traced or followed. ''South.''

'''untraced''' (un-trāst′), ''a.'' '''1.''' Not traced; not followed.—'''2.''' Not marked by footsteps. ''Denham'', Cooper’s Hill.—'''3.''' Not marked out.

'''untracked''' (un-trakt′), ''a.'' '''1.''' Not tracked; not marked by footsteps; pathless: as, ''untracked'' woods. ''Sandys'', tr. of Ovid’s Metamorph., ii.—'''2.''' Not followed by tracking.

'''untractability''' (un-trak-tạ-bil′ị-ti), ''n.'' Intractableness.

'''untractable''' (un-trak′tạ-bl), ''a.'' '''1.''' Not tractable; intractable.
{{smaller block|To speak with libertie, and to say you the truth, they say al in this Court that you are a verie good christian, and a verie ''untractable'' bishop.
{{right|''Guevara'', Letters (tr. by Hellowes, 1577), p. 224.}}}}
readings.c2s3:
{{smaller block|less urged, tutored, disciplined to their work, give way; ''untrained'' nature has no principles.
{{right|''J. H. Newman'', Parochial Sermons, i. 286.}}}}

'''untrammeled, untrammelled''' (un-tram′eld), ''a.'' Not trammeled, hampered, or impeded.

'''untrampled''' (un-tram′pld), ''a.'' Not trampled; not trod upon. ''Shelley.''

'''untransferable''' (un-trȧns-fėr′ạ-bl), ''a.'' Incapable of being transferred or passed from one to another: as, power or right ''untransferable.'' ''Howell'', Pre-eminence of Parliament.

'''untransformed''' (un-trȧns-fôrmd′), ''a.'' Not transformed; unmetamorphosed.

'''untranslatability''' (un-trȧns-lā-tạ-bil′i-ti), ''n.'' The quality of being untranslatable. ''G. P. Marsh'', Lects. on Eng. Lang., xxviii.

'''untranslatable''' (un-trȧns-lā′tạ-bl), ''a.'' Not capable of being translated; also, not fit to be translated. ''Gray'', To West, April, 1742.

'''untranslatableness''' (un-trȧns-lā′tạ-bl-nes), ''n.'' The character of being untranslatable. ''Coleridge.''

'''untranslatably''' (un-trȧns-lā′tạ-bli), ''adv.'' In an untranslatable manner; so as not to be capable of translation. ''Athenæum'', No. 3238, p. 671.

'''untransmutable''' (un-trȧns-mū′tạ-bl), ''a.'' Incapable of being transmuted.
{{smaller block|Each character . . . appears to me in practice pretty durable and ''untransmutable.''
{{right|''Hume.''}}}}

'''untransparent''' (un-trȧns-pãr′ẹnt), ''a.'' Not transparent; opaque: literally or figuratively. ''Boyle'', Works, I. 735.
readings.c3s2:
¶
'''untremblingly''' (un-trem′bling-li), ''adv.'' In an untrembling manner; firmly.

'''untrespassing''' (un-tres′pas-ing), ''a.'' Not trespassing; not transgressing.
{{smaller block|Others were sent more cheerefull, free, and still as it were at large, in the midst of an ''untrespassing'' honesty.
{{right|''Milton'', Apology for Smectymnuus.}}}}

'''untressed†''' (un-trest′), ''a.'' [ME., < ''un-''<sup>1</sup> + ''tressed'', pp. of ''tress''<sup>1</sup>.] With hair unarranged; not done up in tresses, as hair.
{{smaller block|<poem>Hir gilte heres with a golden threde
Ybounden were, ''untressed'' as she lay.</poem>
{{right|''Chaucer'', Parliament of Fowls, l. 268.}}}}

'''untried''' (un-trīd′), ''a.'' '''1.''' Not tried; not attempted.
{{smaller block|<poem>By subtil Stratagems they act their Game,
And leave ''untry’d'' no Avenue to Fame.</poem>
{{right|''Steele'', Conscious Lovers, Prol.}}
<poem>The generous past, when all was possible,
For all was then ''untried''.</poem>
{{right|''Lowell'', Under the Willows.}}}}
'''2.''' Not yet felt or experienced: as, ''untried'' sufferings.
{{smaller block|Remains there yet a plague ''untried'' for me?
{{right|''Beau. and Fl.'', Philaster, iv. 2.}}}}
'''3.''' Not subjected to trial; not tested or put to the test.
{{smaller block|By its perfect shape, its vigor, and its natural dexterity in the use of all its ''untried'' limbs, the infant was worthy to have been brought forth in Eden.
{{right|''Hawthorne'', Scarlet Letter, p. 114.}}}}
'''4†.''' Unnoticed; unexamined.
{{smaller block|<poem>I slide
O’er sixteen years and leave the growth ''untried''.</poem>
{{right|''Shak.'', W. T., iv. 1. 6.}}}}
readings.c3s3:
'''5.''' Not having passed trial; not heard and determined in law: as, the cause remains ''untried.''

'''untrifling''' (un-trī′fling), ''a.'' Not trifling; not indulging in levities. ''Savage.''

'''untrim''' (un-trim′), ''v. t.'' To deprive of trimming; strip; disorder.
{{smaller block|By chance or nature’s changing course ''untrimm’d.''
{{right|''Shak.'', Sonnets, xviii.}}}}

'''untrimmed''' (un-trimd′), ''a.'' '''1.''' Not trimmed; not pruned; not clipped or cut; not put in order: as, an ''untrimmed'' wick; ''untrimmed'' leaves of a book.
{{smaller block|<poem>So let thy tresses, flaring in the wind,
''Untrimmed'' hang about thy bared neck.</poem>
{{right|''Tancr. and Gism.'', O. Pl., ii. 221. (''Nares.'')}}}}
'''2†.''' Virgin.
{{smaller block|<poem>The devil tempts thee here,
In likeness of a new ''untrimmed'' bride.</poem>
{{right|''Shak.'', K. John, iii. 1. 209.}}}}
'''3.''' Not furnished with trimmings.

'''untrimmedness''' (un-trimd′nes), ''n.'' The state of being untrimmed. [Rare.]
{{smaller block|It [an old castle] is not particularly “kept up,” but its quiet rustiness and ''untrimmedness'' only help it to be familiar. {{right|''H. James, Jr.'', Portraits of Places, p. 167.}}}}

'''untriste†''', ''a.'' See ''untrust.''

'''untriumphable†''' (un-trī′um-fa-bl), ''a.'' Admitting no triumph; not an object of triumph. ''S. Butler'', Hudibras.

'''untrodden, untrod''' (un-trod′n, un-trod′), ''a.'' Not having been trod; not passed over; unfrequented. ''Shak.'', J. C., iii. 1. 136.

'''untoiling''' (un-toi′ling), ''a.'' Without toil or labor. ''Thomson'', Castle of Indolence, i. 19.

'''untold''' (un-tōld′), ''a.'' [< ME. ''untold''; < ''un-''<sup>1</sup> + ''told''.] '''1.''' Not told; not related; not revealed. ''Dryden.''—'''2.''' Not numbered; uncounted; that cannot be reckoned: as, money ''untold''.
{{smaller block|In the number let me pass ''untold''.
{{right|''Shak.'', Sonnets, cxxxvi.}}
Anility and Puerility after all are forces, and might do ''untold'' mischief if they were needlessly provoked.
{{right|''J. R. Seeley'', Nat. Religion, p. 129.}}}}

'''untolerable†''' (un-tol′e-ra-bl), ''a.'' Intolerable. ''Bp. Jewell'', Defence of the Apologie, p. 618.

'''untomb''' (un-töm′), ''v. t.'' To take from the tomb; disinter. ''Fuller.''

'''untonality''' (un-tọ̄-nal′i̤-ti), ''n.'' The state of being without definite tonality. ''Amer. Jour. Psychol.'', I. 91. [Rare.]

'''untongue†''' (un-tung′), ''v. t.'' To deprive of a tongue or of a voice; silence.
{{smaller block|Such who commend him in making condemn him in keeping such a diary about him in so dangerous days. Especially he ought to ''untongue'' it from talking to his prejudice.
{{right|''Fuller'', Ch. Hist., XI. ix. 77.}}}}

'''untoomly†''' (un-töm′li), ''adv.'' Hastily.
{{smaller block|<poem>Antenor ''entomly'' turnet his way
Withoutyn lowtyng or lefe, lengit he noght.</poem>
{{right|''Destruction of Troy'' (E. E. T. S.), l. 1822.}}}}

'''untooth''' (un-töth′), ''v. t.'' To deprive of teeth. ''Cowper'', Odyssey, xviii.

'''untoothsome''' (un-töth′sum), ''a.'' Not toothsome; unpalatable. ''Shirley'', Hyde Park, ii. 4.

'''untoothsomeness''' (un-töth′sum-nes), ''n.'' The quality of being untoothsome or unpalatable. ''Bp. Hall'', Contemplations. iii. 287.

'''untormented''' (un-tôr-men′ted), ''a.'' Not tormented; not subjected to torture.
{{smaller block|Of his wo, as who seyth, ''untormented.''
{{right|''Chaucer'', Troilus, i. 1011.}}}}

'''untorn''' (un-tōrn′), ''a.'' Not torn; not rent or forced asunder. ''Cowper.''

'''untouchable''' (un-tuch′a̤-bl), ''a.'' Not capable of being touched; intangible; unassailable.
{{smaller block|''Untouchable'' as to prejudice. ''Feltham'', Resolves, ii. 66.}}

'''untouched''' (un-tucht′), ''a.'' '''1.''' Not touched, in any physical sense; left intact.
{{smaller block|Depart ''untouched.'' {{right|''Shak.'', J. C., iii. 1. 142.}}
<poem>The fresh leaves, ''untouched'' as yet
By summer and its vain regret.</poem>
{{right|''William Morris'', Earthly Paradise, II. 124.}}
The mineral resources [of Texas] are ''untouched.''
{{right|''Warren'', Common School Geography, p. 44.}}}}
'''2.''' Not mentioned; not treated; not examined.
{{smaller block|''Untouched'', or slightly handled, in discourse.
{{right|''Shak.'', Rich. III., iii. 7. 19.}}
We are carried forward to explore new regions of our souls as yet ''untouched'' and untrodden.
{{right|''H. S. Holland'', Logic and Life, p. 50.}}}}
'''3.''' Not affected mentally; not moved; not excited emotionally.
{{smaller block|Wholly ''untouched'' with his agonies. {{right|''Sir P. Sidney.''}}
His heart ’s ''untouch’d'' and whole yet.
{{right|''Fletcher'', Loyal Subject, v. 1.}}
<poem>Time, which matures the intellectual part,
Hath tinged my hairs with grey, but left ''untouched'' my</poem>}}
{{smaller block|heart. {{right|''Southey'' (Reid’s Brit. Poets, II. 158).}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>I, ''untouched'' by one adverse circumstance,
Adopted virtue as my rule of life.</poem>
{{right|''Browning'', Ring and Book, II. 219.}}}}

'''untoward'''<sup>1</sup> (un-tō′ärd), ''a.'' [< ''un-''<sup>1</sup> + ''toward.''] '''1.''' Froward; perverse; refractory; not easily guided or taught.
{{smaller block|This ''untoward'' generation. {{right|Acts ii. 40.}}}}
{{smaller block|What means this scorn, thou most ''untoward'' knave?
{{right|''Shak.'', K. John, i. 1. 243.}}}}
{{smaller block|Nay, look, what a rascally ''untoward'' thing this poetry is.
{{right|''B. Jonson'', Poetaster, i. 1.}}}}
'''2.''' Inconvenient; troublesome; vexatious; unfortunate; unlucky: as, an ''untoward'' event; an ''untoward'' vow.
{{smaller block|An ''untoward'' accident drew me into a quarrel.
{{right|''Sheridan'', The Rivals, v. 1.}}}}
='''Syn. 1.''' ''Wilful, Contrary'', etc. (see ''wayward''), intractable.

'''untoward'''<sup>2</sup>†, ''prep.'' [ME., < ''unto'' + ''-ward.''] Toward.
{{smaller block|<poem>Whan I am my ladie fro,
And thynke ''untowarde'' hir drawe.</poem>
{{right|''Gower'', Conf. Amant., iv.}}}}

'''untowardliness''' (un-tō′ärd-li-nes), ''n.'' The character or state of being untowardly.

'''untowardly''' (un-tō′ärd-li), ''a.'' Awkward; perverse; froward.
{{smaller block|''Untowardly'' tricks and vices. {{right|''Locke'', Education.}}}}

'''untowardly''' (un-tō′ärd-li), ''adv.'' In an untoward, froward, or perverse manner; perversely.
{{smaller block|Matters go ''untowardly'' on our Side in Germany, but the King of Denmark will shortly be in the Field in Person.
{{right|''Howell'', Letters, I. iv. 20.}}}}

'''untowardness''' (un-tō′ärd-nes), ''n.'' The state or character of being untoward; awkwardness; frowardness; perverseness. ''Bp. Wilson.''

'''untractability''' (un-trak-tạ-bil′ị-ti), ''n.'' Intractableness.

'''untractable''' (un-trak′tạ-bl), ''a.'' '''1.''' Not tractable; intractable.
{{smaller block|To speak with libertie, and to say you the truth, they say al in this Court that you are a verie good christian, and a verie ''untractable'' bishop.
{{right|''Guevara'', Letters (tr. by Hellowes, 1577), p. 224.}} The high-spirited and ''untractable'' Agrippina.
{{right|''Gifford'', note on Jonson’s Sejanus.}}}}

{{smaller block|There was room among these hitherto ''untractable'' irregularities for the additional results of the theory. {{right|''Whewell.''}}}}
'''2†.''' Difficult; rough.
{{smaller block|<poem>
I
Toil’d out my uncouth passage, forced to ride
The ''untractable'' abyss.
</poem>
{{right|''Milton'', P. L., x. 476.}}}}

'''untractableness''' (un-trak′ta̤-bl-nes), ''n.'' Intractableness.

'''untraded†''' (un-trā′ded), ''a.'' '''1.''' Not resorted to or frequented for the sake of trading: as, an ''untraded'' place. ''Hakluyt’s Voyages'', iii. 682.—'''2.''' Unpractised; inexperienced.
{{smaller block|A people not utterly ''untraded'' . . . in his discipline.
{{right|''J. Udall'', On Luke i.}}}}
'''3.''' Unhackneyed; unusual; not used commonly.
{{smaller block|That I affect the ''untraded'' oath.
{{right|''Shak.'', T. and C., iv. 5. 178.}}}}

'''untrading''' (un-trā′ding), ''a.'' Not engaged in commerce; not accustomed; inexperienced.
{{smaller block|''Untrading'' and unskilful hands. {{right|''Locke.''}}}}

'''untragic''' (un-traj′ik), ''a.'' Not tragic; hence, comic; ludicrous.
{{smaller block|Emblems not a few of the tragic and the ''untragic'' sort.
{{right|''Carlyle'', French Rev., II. v. 12. (''Davies.'')}}}}

'''untrained''' (un-trānd′), ''a.'' Not trained; not disciplined; uneducated; uninstructed.
{{smaller block|<poem>
My wit ''untrain’d'' in any kind of art.
</poem>
{{right|''Shak.'', 1 Hen. VI., i. 2. 73.}}}}

{{smaller block|I cannot say that I am utterly ''untrain’d'' in those rules which best Rhetoricians have giv’n.
{{right|''Milton'', Apology for Smectymnuus.}}}}

{{smaller block|Not only is the multitude fickle, but the best men, unless urged, tutored, disciplined to their work, give way; ''untrained'' nature has no principles.
{{right|''J. H. Newman'', Parochial Sermons, i. 286.}}}}

'''untraveled, untravelled''' (un-trav′e̤ld), ''a.'' '''1.''' Not traveled; not trodden by passengers: as, an ''untraveled'' forest.
{{smaller block|''Untravelled'' parts. {{right|''Sir T. Browne'', Vulg. Err.}}}}
'''2.''' Not having traveled; not having gained experience by travel; hence, provincial; narrow.
{{smaller block|An ''untravelled'' Englishman. ''Addison'', Spectator, No. 407.}}

'''untread''' (un-tred′), ''v. t.'' To tread back; go back through in the same steps; retrace.
{{smaller block|''Untreading'' a good part of the aforesaid alley. {{right|''Sandys'', Travailes (1652), p. 131.}}}}

'''untreasure''' (un-trezh′ṳ̄r), ''v. t.'' '''1.''' To deprive of a treasure.
{{smaller block|They found the bed ''untreasured'' of their mistress. {{right|''Shak.'', As you Like it, ii. 2. 7.}}}}
'''2.''' To bring forth, as treasure; set forth; display. . [Rare in both uses.]
{{smaller block|The quaintness with which he ''untreasured'' . . . the stores of his memory. {{right|''J. Mitford.''}}}}

'''untreatable''' (un-trē′ta-bl), ''a.'' [< ME. ''untretable''; < ''un-''<sup>1</sup> + ''treatable.''] '''1†.''' Unmanageable; inexorable; implacable.
{{smaller block|Thow shalt nat wenen, quod she, that I bere ''untretable'' batayle ayenis fortune. ''Chaucer'', Boëthius, ii. prose 8.}}
'''2†.''' Not practicable. ''Dr. H. More.''—'''3.''' Incapable of being treated, in any sense.

'''untrembling''' (un-trem′bling), ''a.'' Not trembling or shaking; firm; steady. ''J. Philips'', Cider, i.

'''untremblingly''' (un-trem′bling-li), ''adv.'' In an untrembling manner; firmly.
